tweets.full_text: @x-user-1 Targeting the user boundary keeps tests fast. How do you handle flaky async calls in those small tests?

@x-user-11 benchmarks are cute until the agent hits a messy repo, stale docs, flaky tests, and one cursed bash script from 2018. price per token is trivia. cost per correct shipped task is the scoreboard.
If your deploy time drops but your flaky rate spikes, you didn't optimize, you reorganized the chaos. Real speed is boring: isolated tests, deterministic setup, and no ghost in the machine.

The three tests that shared state weren't slow or flaky on their own. They were only slow because they waited on each other's leftovers. Once we gave each shard its own process and database, the six minutes felt almost accidental.

Developer productivity isn't about typing faster.

It’s about:
• Automating repetitive CI/CD chores
• Scripting routine database seeds
• Killing flaky tests immediately

Protect your focus time like your runway depends on it. It does.

#developer #devtools #productivity #saas

we only flag the model currently

usually the PR owner wants to: 1) maintain merge-ability (resolve merge conflicts, CI failures, etc.) -- keep it green, 2) actually try to merge the PR (respond to human/bot comments, fix test failures, file issues on flaky tests, etc.), or 3) wanted to know if the actual PR wonder has responded to their comments

the monitoring that intentd does is to coalesce updates (controls costs), figure out what's actually blocking the merge, and flag the model when things change (e.g. mergeability). If the owner had instructions about, say, "let me know if a human review has landed", the model does have to make that call
@x-user-39 Honest dogfooding question: how do you separate flaky tests from real app bugs? That distinction is exactly where QA agents live or die for us.

Playwright 1.63 adds named test locks: tests can declare a shared lock (e.g. 'user-settings') so they never run concurrently. Use this to stop flaky failures when parallel tests hit the same external service or account.

THE BEST AI CODING AGENT MAY BE THE ONE THAT WORKS ALL NIGHT AND STILL ISN’T ALLOWED TO MERGE.

This repo ops setup is basically a 24/7 engineering night shift.

While you sleep, agents can:

monitor CI,
classify failures,
catch flaky tests,
watch dependencies for CVEs,
write trivial patches,
run the test suite,
and open draft PRs.

Kimi’s swarm can scale the monitoring across up to 300 sub-agents, while Grok handles the actual repo workflow.

But the most important part is the boundary.

Flaky test? Fix it.
Lint failure? Fix it.
Application logic? Stop.
Security-critical change? Escalate.
Merge to production? Human only.

I think that’s a much more useful definition of autonomous coding.

Not:

“AI can change anything while I sleep.”

But:

“AI can make sure I never wake up to something that could’ve been safely handled without me.”

The goal isn’t removing the engineer.

It’s removing the 2AM version of the engineer.
